messages.subject: standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
messages.subject_clean: standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am fitting a toy linear mixed model with a single random generic component, y = Z u + e, with u ~ MVN(0, sigma_a^2 A), where A is known:
fit <- remlf90(fixed=y ~ 1, generic=list(geno.add=list(model.matrix(~ dat$geno.add - 1), A)), data=dat, method="ai")

With the commands "summary(fit)" and "sqrt(diag(fit$reml$invAI))", I can see that standard errors of the variance components are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse of the observed information matrix. However, it is known (see here <http://glmm.wikidot.com/faq>) that this way of calculating std errors isn't suitable for variance components whose std errors often happen to be asymmetric.

The R package "lme4" allows to estimate the standard errors of variance components via likelihood profiling. Is it available in breedR? Isn't it what is already described in this <https://github.com/famuvie/breedR/wiki/Heritability#case-1-explicit-genetic-component-with-method-ai> wiki page as "simulation from the asymptotic Gaussian joint sampling distribution of the variance components" citing Meyer and Houle (2013)? If yes, could it be made available for generic variance components?

Cheers,
Tim

However, it is known (see here <http://glmm.wikidot.com/faq>) that this way of calculating std errors isn't suitable for variance components whose std errors often happen to be asymmetric.

True. It is a common (for simplicity) approximation.
Often a bad one. But if variances are high enough, it is fine for most purposes.

>
> The R package "lme4" allows to estimate the standard errors of variance components via likelihood profiling. Is it available in breedR?

No, it is not. You need to make ML inference for that, since it is based on a LRT statistic.

> Isn't it what is already described in this <https://github.com/famuvie/breedR/wiki/Heritability#case-1-explicit-genetic-component-with-method-ai> wiki page as "simulation from the asymptotic Gaussian joint sampling distribution of the variance components" citing Meyer and Houle (2013)?

No, it is not the same procedure. But has the same purpose.

> If yes, could it be made available for generic variance components?

It is available. See case 2.1. You need to manually specify you formula for heritability using `se_covar_function`.

Let me know if it works, or if you need any help.
I am aware that the specification of the formula is not precisely "user-friendly" :)

ƒacu.-

messages.subject: Re: [breedR] standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
messages.subject_clean: [breedR] standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
messages.body_plain:
No silly questions here.

What happens is that when you ask for profile confindence intervals for a model fitted with REML is that ir refits the model using ML behind the scenes, and then computes the confindence intervals for the ML estimators (see http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org/lMMwR/lrgprt.pdf, section 1.5.1).

You can see this with a simple experiment:
 ## REML fit
 fm01 <- lmer(Yield ~ 1|Batch, Dyestuff, REML = TRUE)

 ## REML estimates of variance components
 VarCorr(fm01)   # Note sigma_Batch ~ 42
 #>  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
 #>  Batch    (Intercept) 42.001
 #>  Residual             49.510

 ## (narrow) profile confidence intervals
 confint(fm01, method = "profile", optimizer = "Nelder_Mead", level = 0.01)
 #> Computing profile confidence intervals ...
 #>                 49.5 %     50.5 %
 #> .sig01        37.07679   37.44472
 #> .sigma        49.42067   49.59980
 #> (Intercept) 1527.27821 1527.72179

 ## Note how the confidence interval for Batch (.sig01) is around 37.2
 ## Guess what is the ML estimate of Batch?
 VarCorr(lmer(Yield ~ 1 | Batch, Dyestuff, REML = FALSE))
 #>  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
 #>  Batch    (Intercept) 37.26
 #>  Residual             49.51

So, to recap. Likelihood-profiled confidence intervals are based on Likelihood Ratio Tests, which in turn require ML inference. Thus, I can’t provide profile CIs in breedR because I can only perform REML inference. Alternatively, you can use the simulation approach that you mentioned before, in order to avoid the (admittedly) inaccurate estimates of Standard Errors for variance parameters.

ƒacu.-

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot! I read Bates' book a while ago and forgot about it. After reading it again (as well as looking at your example below), I understand why one wants to use REML to estimate variance components, and why one has to use ML to get confidence intervals via likelihood profiling. In the end, it seems strange to end up reporting a REML estimate for a varcomp along its ML intervals. But I guess it is a small detail often ignored in practice.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Vincent!

They indeed discuss bootstrapping, but emphasize that it is "prohibitively time-consuming". That's where they innovate, in "developing a fast analytical approximation depending only on the eigenvalues of the kinship matrix".

Unfortunately, they only looked at the model most-often used by human geneticists, y = X beta + Z u + e with u ~ MVN(0, sigma_u^2 K) and e ~ MVN(0, sigma^2 I), whereas animal/plant geneticists often need other random effects. Their analytical approx may not be (easily) extendable to such cases.

Anyway, for the moment I gather from all this that the solution from Meyer and Houle (2013), available in breedR via "se_covar_function", is a quick(er) alternative to bootstrap.

Facu, is there a way to change the number of samples used by "se_covar_function". I see in the AIREMLF90 manual that we can use "samples_se_covar_function <n>", but I guess it is not (yet) available via breedR? Should I create an issue as a "low priority enhancement"?

messages.subject: joint use of additive and dominance genomic relationship matrices as generic components
messages.subject_clean: joint use of additive and dominance genomic relationship matrices as generic components
messages.body_plain:
Hello, me again,

I learned how to use one generic component <https://github.com/famuvie/breedR/wiki/Overview#generic-component>, but can't succeed in working with two.

Here are some details:
I simulated genotypes via the coalescent for I individuals.
Then, I used the "classical" formulas from Vitezica et al (2013) to estimate the additive and dominance genomic relationship matrices, A and D.
Finally, I simulated phenotypes with Q replicates per individual (several years), for a total of N = Q x I observations, according to y = W c + Z a + Z d + e, where y and e are Nx1, c is Qx1 (fixed-effects), a and d are Ix1, with a ~ MVN_I(0, sigma_a^2 A), d ~ MVN_I(0, sigma_d^2 D) and e ~ MVN_N(0, sigma_e^2 Id). i used values sigma_a^2 = 15, sigma_d^2=0 or 3, and sigma_e^2 = 5.

I then use breedR like this:

fit <- remlf90(fixed=response ~ 1 + year,

               generic=list(geno.add=list(model.matrix(~ modelAD$dat$geno - 1), A),

                            geno.dom=list(model.matrix(~ modelAD$dat$geno - 1), D))),

               data=modelAD$dat,

               method="ai")))

When I simulate with A only, and fit with A ("ai"), the varcomp estimates are fine: hat{sigma}_a^2 ~= 15 and hat{sigma}_e^2 ~= 5.
When I simulate with A and D, and fit with A only ("ai"), the estimate of sigma_a^2 is over-estimated, as expected: hat{sigma}_a^2 ~= 20 and hat{sigma}_e^2 ~= 4.
When I simulate with A and D, and fit with A and D ("ai"), all varcomp estimates are completely off: hat{sigma}_a^2 = hat{sigma}_d^2 ~= 1.00e-10 and hat{sigma}_e^2 ~= 1.49e+06
When I simulate with A and D, and fit with A and D ("em"), varcomp estimates are not all fine: hat{sigma}_a^2 = hat{sigma}_d^2 ~= 10 and hat{sigma}_e^2 ~= 5.

What did I do wrong?

ps: A and D are strongly correlated along their diagonal, but the pattern is quite different for their off-diagonal values; moreover, A is singular, but not D

Mmmm, looks very much like lack of identifiability.

Can you check `cov2cor(fit$reml$invAI)` (from the model fiitted with AI) and confirm that the correlation between geno.add and geno.dom is near 1 (or -1)?

If so, you are doing nothing wrong. There is just not enough info in the data to tell apart the dominance and the additive effects.

You would need to go Bayesian and sort out the confusion using sensible priors.

ƒacu.-
